A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REC, RSE and RLSE research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison. Appendices A–H are retained in v3, which adds Appendix I; the shorter document mainly reflects reformatting.

before.justification: v2 reports original Gaussian-bandit simulations averaged over 300 runs, with regret curves in Figure 1 and numerical results in Table 2.

after.justification: v3 reports updated simulations in Section 8 and additional hyperparameter, horizon-scaling and linear-bandit results in Appendix I.

M1.justification: The REC, RSE and RLSE procedures, confidence-bound formulas and elimination mechanisms are retained. Corrections to the explanations of confidence-bound roles and exploitation clarify the existing algorithms; revised experimental tuning does not introduce a new method component.

E1.justification: The two original Gaussian-bandit instances remain. Appendix I.3 adds one synthetic linear-bandit instance with five arms and two-dimensional features. The hyperparameter and horizon experiments otherwise reuse the original task coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparison retains RASMAB, REC, RSE and UCB1. The new linear-bandit experiment compares RLSE against RSE implemented using one-hot features, adding a comparison absent from v2.

E3.justification: Section 8 changes the reported RSE tuning from one common factor to separate commitment and individual-elimination factors. Appendix I substantially expands the evaluation design through exploration-scale sweeps, horizons of 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000, and a linear-feature comparison. These additions go beyond disclosing settings for existing results.

E4.justification: Appendix I adds several analyses absent from v2: sensitivity of regret and nonreplication to exploration scaling, regret scaling with the horizon, and the benefit of linear features relative to one-hot encoding. Figures 2–3 and Table 4 provide evidence for these distinct questions.

E5.justification: Both versions report 300 runs, the same empirical nonreplication estimator, and two-sigma intervals using plug-in variance in Table 2. No new seed information, repeated-run procedure or uncertainty-estimation method is introduced. Changed interval values are result updates.

E6.justification: All eight mean regrets in Table 2 change. On Model 2, RSE/RASMAB change from 1051.6/844.6 to 683.1/883.7, reversing their ranking; Model 1 RASMAB changes from 3614.4 to 1071.3. Appendix I adds sensitivity, horizon and linear-feature findings. Given the revised tuning, these are updated and additional results rather than established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix D replace the sum of per-phase bad-event probabilities with the global bad-event probability in the general bound. Appendix E removes an erroneous epsilon factor, while Appendix F supplies previously omitted RSE derivations and adds an exploitation-correctness argument under the regret good event. These refine existing theory without changing the principal regret rates.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions: asymptotically negligible replicability overhead, the decision-variable framework, REC/RSE/RLSE, and a two-arm lower bound establishing near-optimality. The expanded ending preserves these claims.

C2.justification: v2's brief conclusion becomes a substantive discussion of strict sequence replication, relaxed allocation-count notions, and whether known gaps could remove additional replicability costs. Appendix I also explains nonmonotonic replication behavior through phase stopping. These substantially extend the treatment of mechanisms, applicability boundaries and open limitations.

D1.justification: Footnote 9 specifies separate RSE tuning multipliers and newly states that RASMAB retains samples from previous phases; v2 does not establish the opposite behavior. Appendix I.3 documents the new instance's dimensions, parameter vector, means, noise and horizon. The runtime and hardware description remains unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 9 adds Garivier et al. (2016, 2019) and Jin et al. (2021a, 2021b), extending discussion of batched and explore-then-commit optimality, including known-gap settings. The main positioning against prior replicable-bandit work remains intact. Publication updates to retained references are not new cited works.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order remain. v3 corrects terminology, converts contribution bullets into prose, reorganizes experimental interpretation into Section 8.1, expands the conclusion into Discussion with a practitioner summary, and adds Appendix I. These are localized narrative changes rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a substantially different manuscript layout with denser spacing, revised title and author formatting, running headers and colored cross-references. Algorithms are reformatted and redistributed. Figure 1 changes axis scales and legend placement, while Figures 2–3 and Table 4 add new displays.

improvement.justification: v3 makes the existing work easier to verify through explicit RSE derivations, localized mathematical corrections and clearer experimental documentation. The sensitivity, scalability and feature comparisons, together with substantive applicability discussion, improve supporting evidence and interpretation. These are useful refinements; the main guarantees remain unchanged, and revised tuning prevents treating the changed scores themselves as evidence of a better method.
